top_cluster.headline: The Trump administration signed a civil nuclear cooperation deal with Saudi Arabia allowing U.S. companies to build nuclear power plants there, but Trump then said the deal is conditioned on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel, while experts and critics warn the agreement may lack adequate safeguards against uranium enrichment to weapons-grade levels.
top_cluster.left_framing: Emphasizes proliferation danger and policy contradiction — that the U.S. is bombing Iran's nuclear sites while simultaneously enabling a Gulf monarchy's nuclear program with weak safeguards, and frames Trump's Israel-normalization condition as a destabilizing, last-minute ultimatum that undermines the deal's credibility.
top_cluster.center_framing: Balances the commercial/diplomatic significance of the deal against expert and nonproliferation warnings, generally centering critics' safety concerns (PBS) while also reporting Trump's conditions and rebuttals fairly neutrally (Axios, NPR) without strongly editorializing either direction.
top_cluster.right_framing: Frames the deal as a diplomatic win, using Trump's own statements to rebut proliferation critics — emphasizing that enrichment is excluded and that the Israel-normalization requirement is a deliberate lever to expand the Abraham Accords, portraying the accords favorably.
top_cluster.left_omissions: Left coverage largely omits Trump's own direct rebuttal (reported by Axios/Breitbart) that the deal explicitly bars enrichment, instead centering critics' warnings that enrichment 'might' be permitted.
top_cluster.right_omissions: Right-leaning coverage omits the expert/nonproliferation warnings and the contradiction with concurrent U.S. military action against Iran's nuclear program that left and center-left outlets emphasize heavily.

blindspot_narrative: Left-only coverage today clusters around institutional accountability and civil-liberties themes (a fired U.S. attorney suing, Cop City surveillance, family separation, Epstein-adjacent congressional testimony) while systematically ignoring Democratic Party internal-dysfunction stories. Right-only coverage clusters around Democratic Party weakness, immigration/voter-fraud, and national-security hawkishness, while ignoring Trump-administration accountability stories entirely. The two information ecosystems are running almost fully separate news cycles today, converging only on the Saudi nuclear story and, partially, on NJ voting — suggesting each side is avoiding stories that complicate its preferred midterm narrative rather than genuinely lacking access to the same facts.
